claims.text: Retention or loss of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by grain-boundary embrittlement caused by thermally induced elemental segregation.
Controlled thermal aging causes segregation-prone elements to accumulate at grain boundaries.
Segregated elements nucleate brittle phases at grain boundaries.
The formation of brittle grain-boundary phases reduces toughness.
The homogenized as-cast or solution-treated starting alloy has a uniform elemental distribution.
The starting alloy has ductile grain boundaries.
Increasing thermal-aging duration promotes diffusion and grain-boundary segregation.
Elevated temperatures below melting or full intermetallic-transformation temperatures can activate elemental diffusion.
Thermal aging changes grain-boundary chemistry and produces secondary brittle phases through enrichment of segregating elements.
Segregation of alloying elements lowers grain-boundary cohesion.
Brittle intergranular phases cause premature crack initiation and propagation.
Premature intergranular crack initiation and propagation diminish overall toughness.
Aged samples will have lower room-temperature toughness than the as-homogenized baseline.
Longer aging times will produce greater grain-boundary segregation.
Greater grain-boundary segregation will correlate with a larger reduction in toughness.
The as-cast or solution-treated baseline has high toughness because its grain boundaries are ductile.
The proposed mechanism applies to initially single-phase high-entropy alloys subjected to aging that induces moderate diffusion.
Alloys with strong elemental ordering or complete aging-induced phase transformation may not follow the proposed mechanism.
